Web design in Waco, TX for a town with two kinds of customers

Most towns of Waco's size, roughly 145,000 residents in 2023 according to Census figures, sell mainly to the people who live there. Waco has a second crowd. Local reporting in 2021 put the city's average at more than two million visitors a year since 2016, a surge driven largely by Magnolia Market at the Silos downtown. Add Baylor University's students and their families, and a Waco business can be talking to three very different people in one afternoon.

Good web design in Waco, TX has to handle that. A resident wants to know you are nearby and reliable. A visitor wants to know you are open right now and how to get there. A Baylor parent wants to know whether you are worth the drive across town. Maurice Johnson writes your pages with those readers in mind, and builds a demo before you pay for anything.

Where Waco does business

Waco sits on Interstate 35 between Dallas and Austin, which puts a steady stream of travelers on the highway past the city every day. Downtown and the area around the Silos draw most of the visitors. Across the Brazos River, East Waco's Elm Avenue reopened to traffic in September 2023 after roughly four years of reconstruction from MLK Boulevard to Spring Street, with new sidewalks, drainage and streetscape. Business owners there said the long closures hurt sales, and the reopening came with new hotels and renovated older buildings planned along the street.

Beyond downtown, the everyday economy looks like any growing Texas city: home services and contractors across Waco and the suburbs of Woodway, Hewitt and Robinson, medical and dental offices, auto shops, salons, restaurants, and businesses that serve the university.

What that means online is simple. Visitors do not know your street, so your site has to tell them clearly. Locals know the street but compare you with the shop across it, so your site has to give them a reason. And both groups are searching on a phone.

Baylor shapes the calendar more than outsiders expect. Move-in week, football Saturdays and commencement bring families who need a place to eat, a hotel nearby, a locksmith, a tire shop or a pharmacy, usually in a hurry and usually on a phone. A business near campus or along the highway that shows up clearly in those moments gets customers who may come back every semester for four years.

What visitors and locals look for on a Waco website

A visitor in town for the weekend

  • Open now? Hours at the top, kept current.
  • How far? An address and a map that opens in their phone.
  • What is it like? Real photos of the inside and the food or work.
  • Can I call? A phone button that works with one tap.

A Waco resident comparing options

  • Do you serve my part of town? Areas named plainly.
  • What exactly do you do? A page for each main service.
  • Who are you? An about page with real people and a real story.
  • What do others say? Your Google reviews, shown on the site with Pro.

In the Ubersuggest export used to plan this site, "web design Waco TX" shows around 50 monthly searches and an SEO difficulty of just 14. That is a modest local search, which is normal for a city this size, and a reminder that the searches your own customers make for your trade are the ones that matter most.

Three website problems that cost a Waco business customers

Hours that are wrong on the busiest days. Waco's calendar has peaks: Baylor move-in and graduation weekends, home football games, holiday shopping, and the steady flow of weekend visitors. A site that still shows last year's holiday hours, or no hours at all, sends a visitor to the next result. Updates are included with hosting and maintenance, so changing them is a quick email to Maurice, not a project.

A Facebook page doing a website's job. Plenty of good Waco businesses live entirely on social media. That works for regulars who already follow you. It does very little for someone typing your trade into Google from a hotel room off I-35, because Google has almost nothing to show them.

One page trying to serve everybody. A single home page that lists every service in a paragraph cannot match the specific searches people make. A page for each main service, and a page for each town you work in, gives each search a clear answer. That is the whole idea behind the service area page in Starter and the city pages in Pro.

Each of these is easy to check on your own site tonight. Open it on your phone, look up your hours, and search your trade plus "Waco" to see what a stranger would find.

None of these takes a large budget to fix. They take somebody sitting down to write the pages properly, which is the part of the job Maurice does by hand.

Straight answer on location: Dominion Web Design Pro has no office in Waco. Maurice Johnson builds every site from Big Sandy in East Texas and delivers it remotely, by link, phone and email.

Free small business help in Waco

Dominion Web Design Pro has no arrangement with any of these. Each is worth a call.

McLennan SBDC

The Small Business Development Center at McLennan Community College offers free, confidential advising and affordable training for businesses in McLennan, Bell, Bosque, Coryell, Falls, Hill and Johnson counties.

Greater Waco Chamber

The city's main chamber of commerce, which helps entrepreneurs find resources and works with Start Up Waco on new businesses.

Cen-Tex Hispanic and African American chambers

Two more chambers serving Central Texas business owners, both listed by the City of Waco among its economic development partners.

Which package suits a Waco business

A shop, cafe or studio near downtown that mostly needs to be found and called is a Starter site. Five pages, one of them about the area you serve, written by hand and usually online between day 7 and day 14. A contractor or home service company working across McLennan County is a Pro site, with the 10 city pages doing the work in the suburbs. A business with several services across Central Texas, say from Temple to Hillsboro, is the Agency case, where keyword research decides which pages get written.

Common questions

How much does web design in Waco, TX cost?

Here it is one of three fixed amounts. $497 buys a five-page Starter site. $997 buys Pro, which has ten pages plus ten city pages for towns such as Woodway or Hewitt. $1,997 buys Agency, where research across Central Texas decides how many pages get written. None of them is a payment plan. The ongoing cost is $49 a month for hosting and maintenance, which drops away if you keep the AI agent, since that plan covers it.

Do Waco businesses need a website if most customers are local?

Most do, because local customers still check online before they call or drive over. And Waco has a second audience: visitors who arrive knowing nothing about the town and search on their phones for food, shopping, repairs and services. A site with your hours, location and a one-tap phone button catches both.

Can a Waco website also cover Woodway, Hewitt and the rest of McLennan County?

Yes. If you serve Woodway, Hewitt, Robinson, Bellmead, Lacy Lakeview or McGregor, the Pro package's 10 city pages can give each of those places its own page, written for that town rather than copied from the Waco page.

Are you based in Waco?

No. Dominion Web Design Pro works from Big Sandy in East Texas and builds Waco sites remotely. The free demo reaches you as a link, questions get handled over the phone, and page approvals come through email.
